item.title: Jerry Liu：Introducing the Document Parsing Protocol (DPP)
item.description:
Introducing the Document Parsing Protocol (DPP)

There are hundreds of different OCR models and tools, but they might all parse a document in different ways.

Some errors are very clear-cut (e.g. hallucinating text, or completely misaligning a table), but many errors are much more ambiguous (e.g. how to represent split tables sharing a header). It's an issue that plagues most parse benchmarks too, because they inherently reward a certain style even if other styles might be semantically correct.

We introduce a protocol that proposes a standard way of parsing these documents into a correct format. We've curated a list of 140 rules that cover literally every aspect of doc parsing, for instance:
- tables: borderless whitespace tables, header-only tables, horizontal slicing, side-by-side mini tables
- forms: key-value regions, checkboxes, checklists, ids and labels, fields outside the form,
- charts: standardized chart output, multiple charts, gantt charts, line charts

You can use DPP as an evaluation rubric for LLMs when determining the quality of parsing a document.

It's not a full evaluation benchmark (yet), but an initial evaluation guide, and meant to encourage a discussion on what are the "best" ways to parse a document.

Check it out: https://t.co/HsLh6ma9bB

Blog: https://t.co/0md2O2M2Mf

item.title: Jerry Liu：GPT 6.1 Terra is a strong frontier model baseline for document parsing.
item.description:
GPT 6.1 Terra is a strong frontier model baseline for document parsing.

✅ It spikes at table parsing, coming in 5th on our overall leaderboard, ahead of 6 Sol and behind Opus 5.5 / Astra
✅ It is decent at content faithfulness and reading order
✅ It struggles on layout, charts, and formatting

Coming in at ~1c per page, it's not a bad option for table-heavy pages! You can use these alongside specialized OCR solutions (like LlamaParse) that will give more consistent performance across a variety of dimensions.

Check it out on ParseBench: https://t.co/PWczfhp0OX

item.title: Jerry Liu：Document extraction is an arbitrarily complex reasoning problem for both frontie…
item.description:
Document extraction is an arbitrarily complex reasoning problem for both frontier models and humans.

✅ The schema encodes essentially hundreds of interrelated reasoning tasks
✅ A PDF can be hundreds or even thousands of pages - it’s an open-world information environment for LLMs to explore (similar to why gdp.pdf is hard)
✅ Solving even a single task is a hard reasoning problem over this environment, where the right dependencies must be reasoned over
✅ The information can be scattered across extraordinarily complex dimensions, from sections, tables, charts, diagrams, handwriting, and more.

Document work is a microcosm of knowledge work as a whole. We’re invested in developing the hardest benchmarks that reflect real-world professional work, challenge the capabilities of frontier models, and incentivize specialized model development for document work.

We released ExtractBench Pro today. Check out the below example as an example of a reasoning task that requires finding the right constraints, then pulling information from tables. https://t.co/bwxs86iS1d

ExtractBench Pro: https://t.co/qrr3C1imM2

item.title: Jerry Liu：Introducing ExtractBenchPro: the most challenging benchmark for real-world docum…
item.description:
Introducing ExtractBenchPro: the most challenging benchmark for real-world document extraction.

We see a massive long tail of document complexity in terms of use cases brought on from our customers, that are completely unsolved from a price-performance standpoint. These include trial balances, well logs, canvass binders, site plan reviews, duty reconciliations, loss runs, and more.

Most existing extraction benchmarks are saturated by the frontier models (our cheapest modes now score 93%+ on ExtractBench). So there is enormous economic value in building a complex extraction benchmark that reflects this long-tail of knowledge work.

We spent a long time curating the most complex elements that we saw from real world extraction use cases:
✅ Document conventions: containing legends or rules where the rest of the document should be interpreted
✅ Density of internal jargon: specific definitions that must be cross-referenced within a doc
✅ Aggregation and reasoning: beyond returning exact values on a page, infer values derived from aggregating multiple sources of information
✅ Drawn relations: complex diagrams like procedures and circuits
✅ Charts inside documents: read precise points within a chart
✅ Long chart sheets: some data series like well logs cram all this data into an extremely long page

Within the industries where document extraction is relevant, even small mistakes can have enormous negative impacts. Therefore our headline evaluation metric is based on perfect documents: the proportion of docs with perfect (100%) value f1 score.
(Besides this we also measure value f1 and grounded f1)

It’s an extremely hard task for even the latest frontier models to solve, topping out at ~58% or so in Value F1 score for Codex with Astra - which is quite good but extremely expensive (almost $1 per page!) Our LlamaParse agentic/agentic plus modes are 20-40% and cover the left side of the Pareto frontier, at price ranges that are feasible for full production use.

ExtractBenchPro is available today as a website/technical blog, and also on Github and HuggingFace. Check it out!

Blog: https://t.co/bwxs86iS1d
Website: https://t.co/uRrFNU1Fqo
Hugging Face: https://t.co/1VImPRTorq
Github (is ExtractBench): https://t.co/auzmOGhsaB

item.title: Jerry Liu：These days, you can pretty much solve any task by defining an eval and hillclimb…
item.description:
These days, you can pretty much solve any task by defining an eval and hillclimbing over it, instead of directly defining the deterministic/agentic workflow to solve it.

The data provider companies' entire job is to define evals for all economic activity to make the frontier models capable of doing anything.

Your job then becomes pointing frontier intelligence in the right direction - defining what to solve, and how to measure what good looks like.

Agent application interfaces will evolve to capture this. The most complex processes will still need some sort of explicit workflow builder interface, but most tasks can be compressed into goals and eval instructions.

item.title: Jerry Liu：Today I’m excited to introduce OpenDocRouter - a unified API for document parsin…
item.description:
Today I’m excited to introduce OpenDocRouter - a unified API for document parsing with the latest frontier and open-weight models.

There are a lot of VLMs and OCR models that can be used for document parsing: we have over 130+ models on ParseBench, and a HuggingFace search for “ocr” turns up thousands of results.

It’s extremely time consuming to choose between OCR vendors. You need to figure out the right prompts, handle rate limits, manage deployments, integrations with all models you’re using, and benchmark new models as they come out.

OpenDocRouter provides a comprehensive, transparent set of models along the price-performance frontier. It manages a unified API to transcribe documents to markdown. It serves all frontier and open-weight models “at-cost”, with a small transaction cut. It handles rate limits with all models to ensure you can put massive volume through. It even offers bounding boxes and layout as a service, so that you can add grounding to any model that you’re using.

When new OCR candidate models ship, we will benchmark them on ParseBench and immediately add them to OpenDocRouter.

We’re adding a lot more models very quickly, and also adding some extremely exciting feature improvements (e.g. automated routing) as we speak.

We welcome your feedback!

Check it out: https://t.co/v8PieWWUNV

Blog: https://t.co/ilVqqJRacP

A properly tuned agentic OCR needs to dynamically apply extra compute to complex elements, review and correct failures, and create the right semantic meaning throughout the page. It's a task that frontier models are both overengineered for in terms of cost and latency, and struggle at over a long tail of complex edge cases.

item.title: jerryjliu0：Yesterday I hosted a fun dinner conversation with @vincentsunnchen from @Snorke…
item.description:
Yesterday I hosted a fun dinner conversation with @vincentsunnchen from @SnorkelAI on evals and RL environments.

The "data and RL env" companies (like Snorkel) have seen massive growth in the past few years. There's been an explosion of interest in evals. At the same time, models are ripping through benchmarks with each new release. We talked about the evals everyone is defining, what evals are still left unsolved, what’s left up to frontier models vs. intelligence that you own, and more:

- A big challenge for building RL environments is “fairness” - when the model fails on a given environment, can you attribute it to the input, harness, or reward model?

- Building proper rewards is hard. Some tasks are not easily quantifiable. You also want to discourage reward hacking. At the same time, you don’t want to be too prescriptive with intermediate rewards.

- Long horizon evals are still extremely hard, some business processes can take up to weeks or months before the final outcome

- Most regulated industries still need human in the loop to guarantee ~100% accuracy, “80%” accuracy is not good enough

- As models get more intelligent, there will be a barbell of boutique data vendors (e.g. any SMB) any scaled up data providers.

- Models still exhibit “jagged intelligence” where they still fail on a long tail of edge cases.

- There might always be opportunities to gather unique data for a given task and posttrain models for lower cost and higher accuracy.

This marks #003 in our founder dinner series. What topic should we discuss next? Let us know your thoughts below!
